name: Internal Family Systems (IFS)
founded_year_range: 1982-1987. The model was developed in the 1980s, the Guilford textbook appeared in 1995, and the Center for Self Leadership was founded in 2000 and renamed the IFS Institute in 2019.
cost_summary: Patients pay ordinary therapy fees, about US$120-250 per session and often private pay. The No Bad Parts book costs about US$20. Per The Nation (2025), clinician training costs US$3,990-5,300 for Level 1 and nearly US$10k to reach Level 3. Retreats run about US$7,000-8,500. The IFS Online Circle course costs US$497 per cohort (Spring and Fall 2026 cohorts), and other Institute online courses cost US$245-397.
mechanisms: parts/Self multiplicity: protective parts (managers, firefighters) shielding burdened exiles
mechanism_summary: The mind is made up of sub-personalities ("parts") around an undamaged core Self. Trauma loads exiled parts with burdens. Protective managers and firefighters keep that pain out of awareness, and their extreme strategies produce psychiatric symptoms. IFS authors also propose that they produce or amplify bodily symptoms such as pain, fatigue, gut symptoms and inflammation. Healing comes from unblending from protectors, accessing Self, then witnessing and unburdening exiles. One model is applied across all conditions, and IFS offers no pain-neuroscience or central-sensitisation model of its own.
roots: Transactional Analysis ego states / Gestalt empty chair
techniques: 6 Fs unblending (find, focus, flesh out, feel toward, befriend, fear)
mainstream_notes: IFS is very widely used by psychotherapists: 45,764 Psychology Today profiles mentioned it in April 2024 (Brownstone et al. 2024). SAMHSA NREPP listed it in 2015, rating it effective for general functioning and wellbeing and promising for anxiety, depression, physical health and resilience, mainly on the strength of the RA trial. NREPP closed in 2018. The PARTS programme was developed at Cambridge Health Alliance, a Harvard affiliate. IFS is not in NICE, APA or VA/DoD guidelines and is not standard in pain clinics.
insurance_notes: IFS can be billed as generic psychotherapy (CPT 90834/90837) by licensed in-network clinicians. There is no modality-specific coverage, and many IFS therapists are private pay. Training, courses and retreats are not covered.

key_trials.citation: Shadick NA, Sowell NF, ... Schwartz RC. J Rheumatol 2013;40(11):1831-41. doi:10.3899/jrheum.121465
key_trials.design: Proof-of-concept RCT: 9-month IFS vs mailed education, both arms with usual RA care (NCT00869349)
key_trials.finding: Post-treatment, IFS improved overall pain (p=0.04) and physical function (p=0.04). At 1 year, self-rated joint pain, depression and self-compassion remained better. There was no sustained improvement in anxiety, self-efficacy or disease activity. The developer was a co-author.

key_trials.citation: Haddock SA, Weiler LM, Trump LJ, Henry KL. J Marital Fam Ther 2017;43(1):131-44. doi:10.1111/jmft.12184
key_trials.design: Pilot RCT: IFS vs treatment as usual (CBT/IPT) for depressed female college students
key_trials.finding: 37 were randomised and 17 vs 15 analysed. Depression fell in both arms, with no significant difference between groups in the size or rate of change.

key_trials.citation: Hodgdon HB, Anderson FG, Southwell E, Hrubec W, Schwartz R. J Aggress Maltreat Trauma 2022;31(1):22-43 (online 2021). doi:10.1080/10926771.2021.2013375
key_trials.design: Uncontrolled pilot: 16 x 90-min individual sessions for PTSD after multiple childhood trauma
key_trials.finding: Large pre-post reductions in PTSD, depression, dissociation and somatisation. At 1-month follow-up, 12 of 13 PTSD-diagnosed completers no longer met criteria. The developer was a co-author.

key_trials.citation: Comeau et al. (senior author Schuman-Olivier Z). Psychol Trauma 2024;16(Suppl 3):S636-40. PMID 38934934
key_trials.design: Single-arm feasibility study of PARTS: 16 x 90-min online IFS groups plus 8 individual sessions
key_trials.finding: 73% attended at least 12 groups, and 92% of responders would recommend it. PTSD severity fell (d=-0.7 at week 16, -0.9 at week 24).

key_trials.citation: Joss D, Comeau A, ... Sweezy M, Schuman-Olivier Z. Psychol Trauma 2026 (online 29 Jan 2026). doi:10.1037/tra0002089. PMID 41609644
key_trials.design: RCT: PARTS online group IFS vs Nature-Based Stress Reduction for Trauma Survivors (matched active control), each with 16 weekly groups plus 8 individual sessions (NCT05095428)
key_trials.finding: Both arms had large CAPS-5 reductions (p<.001), with no significant difference between arms. PARTS had higher attendance and satisfaction. A Sci Rep 2026 secondary analysis (PMID 42471454) links shared benefit to reduced isolation. Funded by the Foundation for Self Leadership.

key_trials.citation: Ally et al. Front Psychiatry 2025;16:1544435. doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2025.1544435
key_trials.design: Single-arm pilot of online group IFS (PARTS-SUD: 12 weekly groups plus 6 individual sessions) for comorbid PTSD and substance use
key_trials.finding: Retention was 70%. PCL-5 fell by about 1.7 points per week, and 54% reached the minimally important difference.

key_trials.citation: Habibi N, Basharpoor S, Atadokht A, Narimani M, Hatami Varzaneh A. Child Abuse Negl 2026;178:108140. doi:10.1016/j.chiabu.2026.108140. PMID 42241954
key_trials.design: Randomised pre-post-follow-up group study (described as quasi-experimental): IFS-based group vs control for trauma-exposed adolescents in out-of-home care, Iran
key_trials.finding: Reduced post-traumatic cognitions (negative self-cognitions eta-squared 0.40) and fear of compassion, maintained at 2-month follow-up. Independent of the IFS Institute; control condition not described in the abstract.

controversy:
Critics say the 'evidence-based' marketing outstrips a small, mostly developer-affiliated evidence base (Brownstone et al., Psychotherapy Bulletin 2024; McAllen, The Nation 2025). A 2025 scoping review (Buys, Clinical Psychologist) found only 2 RCTs among 27 studies. Other concerns:
- Splitting into parts may destabilise clients with psychosis or dissociation.
- Unburdening may risk false or recovered memories.
- The Cut (Rachel Corbett, 30 Oct 2025) reported that Richard Schwartz consulted at Castlewood, where four patients (Nasseff, Thompson, Travers, Taylor) sued co-founder Mark Schwartz (unrelated) over implanted false memories; the suits were settled, and a former research director said Richard "knew fully what was going on". The IFS Institute disputes this (response of 4 Nov 2025), saying he was never a treating therapist there and was never named in any suit.
- Spiritual and 'exorcism'-like content ('unattached burdens') has drawn criticism.
- Attributing autoimmune or chronic symptoms to parts risks blaming patients.
- Critics point to commercialised tiered training, recertification fees and costly retreats.

indicators.metric: Psychology Today therapist profiles mentioning IFS

indicators.value: ~3 million 'Internal Family Systems Therapy'; 1.2M 'Internal Family Systems Technique'
No Bad Parts (Sounds True, 2021), bestseller with an audiobook featuring Alanis Morissette
full-time staff grew from 12 to 35; trainers from 30 to more than 100

popularity.reach_estimate: Several million people. Tens of thousands of trained clinicians (nearly 4,000 per year recently, plus 45k Psychology Today profiles) each see many clients, and books, podcasts and social media reach millions more. Estimate: roughly 1-5 million people have received IFS or IFS-informed therapy or self-help.
popularity.method_notes:
Trajectory anchors:
- Founding in the 1980s, then a niche period through the 1995 Guilford book and the 2000 Center for Self Leadership.
- 2013 RA RCT; 2014 The Body Keeps the Score; 2015 NREPP listing.
- Trainee counts from The Nation: ~500 in 2017, ~1,600 in 2020, nearly 4,000 per year by 2024-25.
- 2021 No Bad Parts plus podcast exposure; 2024 social-media counts from Brownstone et al.
- Critical press in 2025 (The Nation, The Cut) and a slight plateau signal in 2026.
Google Trends was not queried directly; levels are relative and judgement-based. The reach estimate assumes about 30-50k IFS-trained clinicians, each seeing dozens to hundreds of clients over time, plus self-help readers.
